body_markdown:
The leaves are turning, cooler winds are blowing, and the forecast gets grimmer by the week. These are all signs for many classic car owners that it’s time to take stock of their winter storage situation and begin prep for a long season’s nap.


You’ll find plenty of guides out there detailing all the steps you *should* take when putting an older vehicle away for months of downtime—but here, we’re taking the opposite tack. Instead, we present to you a litany of everything you shouldn’t do when storing a car, culled from hard-earned (and in some cases, tear-stained and curse-leavened) experience with our own fleet.


Each of these “don’t-dos” has sadly happened to us. Learn from our mistakes, and you can enjoy a hassle-free and less emotionally charged approach to keeping your vehicle safe and sound all winter long.


## You’re Going to Forget It’s in Gear, So Don’t Take the Risk


Unsplash/Heri Perisetla


If you are storing a vehicle with an automatic transmission, it’s a simple matter to put it in park and walk away for the winter season. If the automobile in question has a manual gearbox, however, things are a little more complicated.


You should always avoid using a parking brake when leaving a car or truck stopped for months at a time. The reason? Especially on older cars, the mechanism that operates the brake can easily seize up if left in place for an extended period. Depending on the design of your brake, it’s also possible for the pads to stick to the discs (especially in more humid environments), or the shoes to do the same inside the drum. This can potentially cause damage while rolling out the following spring when these components attempt to break free of each other (keyword: break, occasionally in dramatic fashion).


Unsplash/Wesley Tingey


It can be tempting to just put the transmission in gear and rely on that to keep it from moving over the course of storage. Here’s where heartbreak number two sets in: it’s extremely easy to forget, months later, that a vehicle is sitting in first, or reverse, when you start it up. No matter how many notes you leave on your phone, or even taped to the steering wheel, there’s simply too much muscle memory to potentially get in the way on restart. The end result? A lurch forward or backward that likely collides with something hard enough to dent your bumper or scratch your paint, and then months of brooding and self-recrimination every time your eye catches the offending scuff.


The answer here is cheap and easy to implement. Deploy a set of wheel chocks front and rear, and you can keep the parking brake off and the transmission in neutral, thus avoiding the pain caused by a springtime memory hole.


## Avoid Storing Your Car in a Greenhouse


Flickr/Doug Bull


Temporary car shelters can be a useful tool in keeping the elements at bay during the colder, wetter, and snowier months of the year. Unfortunately, certain aspects of their design risk transforming your Mylar garage into an automotive greenhouse that will see you harvesting a delightful crop of mildew and moss.


Many car shelters are at least semi-transparent, which makes sense as it helps improve visibility by letting the sun shine through into the area they are protecting. Unfortunately, that same sunlight can heat up the air inside, causing it to rise to the ceiling and condense on the plastic roof, whereupon it starts to drip, drip, drip onto the vehicle below. Even darker-colored shelters can suffer from this temperature differential between the inside and winter’s chill outside, leading to a humid mess that is bad for your vehicle’s paint, finish, and especially its interior.


Unsplash/Parker Coffman


There’s really only one way to avoid transforming a temporary shelter into a tropical rainforest, and that’s by ensuring you have constant ventilation that allows all that moist air to escape into the atmosphere instead of condensing on the ceiling and walls. You can buy portable garages with built-in vents, or you can install them on an existing garage with some scissors and adhesive. In more extreme cases, you might even have to run a small fan to keep air circulating at all times (especially if you’re storing your vehicle near a small body of water or stream—yes, it happened to us).


Temporary shelters aren’t the only car-related structures to suffer from condensation woes. Poorly ventilated garages offer similar dangers, and even carports that are open on all sides can trap moisture with the roof and rain it down on your ride.


## Car Covers Need to Breathe, or, Well, See Above


Norman Garrett


Take everything you just read about condensation and apply it to the car cover you’re using, which is in many ways just a temporary shelter that directly touches a vehicle’s paint.


Unless you’re storing inside a humidity- and temperature-controlled structure, those same temperature differences and fluctuations can cause moisture to condense inside your auto’s cabin, as well as on its paint. If the car cover you’re using is not breathable—i.e., made of a material that allows air to move through it—it can stay there long enough to cause corrosion, or the same mold-friendly conditions that can lead to spores colonizing your vehicle’s interior.


Whether you’re covering indoors or outdoors, don’t cheap out on a vinyl tarp or old bed sheet. Choose a car cover that’s designed for your specific situation and that can breathe all winter long.


## Don’t Assume Your Car Doesn’t Leak


If you don’t hunt down the source of an antifreeze leak, it’ll bite you.


Rob Siegel


Many classic car owners seek a common cause and end up sharing a storage space over the course of the winter. In some cases, these arrangements can end up with vehicles stacked on top of each other, Tetris-style, using simple four-post lifts to maximize the available volume.


You can likely see where this is going. You don’t want the first time you hear about a fluid leak on your car to be in the form of a phone call from the frustrated owner of the vintage Ferrari sitting below it, asking how they’re going to remove the stains from the differential/transmission/engine oil/coolant that’s been gently drizzling all over their roof.


Rob Siegel


Even if the garage floor or driveway asphalt under your car looks spotless, it’s worth it to unroll a length of paper under your car just prior to storage and let it sit for a day or two to see what collects—especially after everything’s been warmed up from a short drive. That way, if necessary, you can ask to be stored on terra firma, or for a drip tray to be deployed to protect both your reputation (and the dignity of your storage-mates).


## Did You Really Use a Full Tank of Fuel Last Season?


Most classic car owners know that modern fuel isn’t stable enough to sit in a tank, untreated, for months on end (especially if it contains high levels of ethanol). There’s an entire industry of additives out there dedicated to keeping fuel stable enough for storage, and while using these inexpensive products is cheap insurance against gasoline breakdown, moisture build-up, and sludge in the tank, there’s one aspect of storing gas over the winter that often gets overlooked: you might actually be putting it away for two winters, not just one.


Wait, what? It all comes down to how much you actually use your car after you bring it out from its hibernation period. It’s common to keep track of oil changes, but not everyone is as rigorous when it comes to knowing how many times they fueled up over the course of the summer.


[Brandan Gillogly](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/brandan-gillogly/)


It might surprise you to find out that you didn’t actually go through a full tank of gas, whether due to vacation travel, repairs, or simply a lack of free time keeping you from doing more than quick trips to the local cruise night or ice cream spot. Or, you might have put $20 into the tank here and there, but never fully used up the previous season’s fuel. This often means there’s some very old gas still swirling around in the tank.


Even if you top up a tank that’s a quarter full of gas dating back more than 12 months, you’re flirting with disaster. That fuel isn’t going to respond to a bottle of stabilizer being dumped in just before storage—in fact, it’s already broken down and created deposits in your fuel system, not to mention added corrosion-causing moisture. The immediate effects can be difficult to detect (an engine stumble here, a hard start there), but over time you’re looking at gummed-up injectors, rust accumulating in your tank and potentially clogging your lines, and, if it happens several years in a row, a need to drain a syrupy mess right from the tank itself.


Luke Sharrett/Bloomberg/Getty Images


Fortunately, there’s a simple solution, and that’s to make sure you run at least a full tank through your motor just before your storage date. Doing so gives you the peace of mind that the only gas you’re sending on a long winter’s nap is the tank you just pumped in a few days before its slumber.


## Learn from Our Sad Mistakes


No one wants to end up a cautionary tale, especially if it involves shelling out extra cash at the end of storage season to fix the kind of issues you thought you were avoiding by putting your vehicle away. Make a checklist before you hang up the keys to ensure you’ve covered the full range of problems you could encounter while your classic is hibernating, and you’ll come out ahead of the game—and, likely, ahead of a few of us.
